q: In a leftmost derivation, each step rewrites…
options: the leftmost variable in the current string
explain: Leftmost derivations always expand the leftmost variable. Rightmost derivations expand the rightmost one.

options: some string has two different parse trees
some string has both a leftmost and a rightmost derivation
it has more than one start symbol
explain: Every derivable string has both an LMD and an RMD, which is normal. Ambiguity means two different trees, or equivalently two different leftmost derivations.

q: With S → S + S | S * S | id, how many different parse trees does id + id * id have?
explain: Either + is at the root, giving id + (id * id), or * is at the root, giving (id + id) * id.

q: In the grammar E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → ( E ) | id, why does * bind tighter than +?
options: * is produced by T, which sits below + in every parse tree
* appears later in the list of rules
explain: Each precedence level has its own variable. A + can only combine T's, and a * is formed inside a T, so * is always grouped first.

q: The grammar S → aS | A, A → aA | b is ambiguous.
explain: True. For 'ab', S ⇒ aS ⇒ aA ⇒ ab and S ⇒ A ⇒ aA ⇒ ab are two different leftmost derivations (two different trees). The language is a*b, and S → aS | b generates it unambiguously.

q: Some context-free languages are inherently ambiguous: every grammar for them is ambiguous.
explain: True. The standard example is {aⁱbʲcᵏ | i = j or j = k}. Strings with i = j = k always get two parse trees.

q: The yield of a parse tree is…
options: the leaves read from left to right
the longest path from root to leaf
explain: Concatenating the leaf labels (terminals, with ε as nothing) left to right gives the derived string.

q: How many leftmost derivations does a single parse tree correspond to?
options: As many as there are variables
It depends on the string length
explain: A parse tree fixes every production used and where. Expanding the leftmost variable each time then gives one specific order. So a string has two trees exactly when it has two LMDs.

q: There is an algorithm that decides, for any context-free grammar, whether it is ambiguous.
explain: False. Ambiguity of CFGs is undecidable in general. You can show that a particular grammar is ambiguous by finding two trees, but no algorithm settles every grammar.

q: In a parse tree, which nodes may have children?
explain: Internal nodes are variables, expanded by a production. Terminals and ε are always leaves.
